ai.literal: Those of evil deeds fear not; the excellent ones will fear the arrogance called evil deed.
ai.translation: Those accustomed to evil do not fear it, but the noble deeply fear the arrogance of committing evil deeds.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்களைச் செய்பவர்கள் தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கைக் கண்டு அஞ்ச மாட்டார்கள். ஆனால் சிறந்த பண்புடையவர்கள் அதற்கு அஞ்சுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts the attitudes of two types of people towards wrongdoing. Those who already commit evil deeds do not fear the arrogance and destructive pride that comes with doing evil. In contrast, noble and excellent people deeply fear this arrogance, knowing its harmful consequences. The word 'cerukku' (arrogance or infatuation) highlights that evil is not just an action, but a blinding pride that the wise actively avoid.

ai.literal: Evil things evil yielding-because, evil things fire-than-even to-fear will-be.
ai.translation: Because evil deeds yield only evil, they are to be feared even more than fire.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்கள் தீமையான விளைவுகளையே தருவதால், அத்தீய செயல்களை நெருப்பை விட அதிகமாகப் பயந்து ஒதுக்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains why one should be terrified of committing evil deeds. The word 'தீயவை' refers to bad actions, which inherently produce 'தீய' or bad outcomes, indicated by 'பயத்தலால்' (because they yield). Because their result is always harmful, the poet compares them to fire ('தீ'). However, evil deeds are said to be feared ('அஞ்சப்படும்') even more than fire, as fire only burns what it touches, while evil deeds bring lasting ruin.

ai.literal: Among wisdom all chief they say, evil things even to those who harm not doing refraining.
ai.translation: They say the foremost of all wisdom is to refrain from doing evil, even to those who harm you.
ai.modern: தமக்குத் தீங்கு செய்பவர்க்கும் தீமையான செயல்களைச் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே எல்லா அறிவுகளிலும் சிறந்த அறிவு என்று கூறுவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the highest form of wisdom in the context of fearing evil deeds. The phrase 'அறிவினுள் எல்லாம் தலை' establishes a hierarchy of knowledge, placing moral restraint at the very top as the 'head' or chief wisdom. The word 'செறுவார்க்கும்' means 'even to those who harm or hate', emphasizing that retaliation is never justified. Finally, 'செய்யா விடல்' highlights that true wisdom is not merely theoretical, but the active, disciplined choice to refrain from committing evil regardless of the provocation.

ai.literal: Even having forgotten, another's ruin let one not plan; if planned, virtue will plan the planner's ruin.
ai.translation: Do not plot the ruin of another, even in a moment of forgetfulness. If you do, virtue itself will plot your ruin.
ai.modern: மறந்துபோய்கூட மற்றொருவனுக்குக் கேடு செய்ய நினைக்கக் கூடாது; அப்படி நினைத்தால், நினைத்தவனுக்குக் கேடு செய்ய அறமே நினைக்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against plotting harm to others, emphasizing that such thoughts should not occur even by accident or forgetfulness. The word 'சூழற்க' (let one not plan) highlights that the mere intention or plotting of evil is forbidden. If one does plot another's ruin, 'அறம்' (virtue or the moral order) will turn against them and actively plan their downfall. Thus, the moral law acts as an inevitable force of justice against those who harbor malicious intentions.

ai.literal: Destitute saying evil things let one not do; if done, destitute he will become again in return.
ai.translation: Do not commit evil deeds thinking you are poor. If you do, you will only become poor again.
ai.modern: நான் வறுமையில் இருக்கிறேன் என்று நினைத்து தீய செயல்களைச் செய்யக்கூடாது. அப்படிச் செய்தால், மீண்டும் வறுமையே வந்து சேரும்.
ai.explanation: The couplet warns against using poverty as an excuse to commit evil deeds. The word 'இலன்' refers to a destitute person. If someone does evil to escape poverty, the inevitable result is that they will be thrown back into an even worse state of destitution. True prosperity cannot be built on evil actions.

ai.literal: Evil things oneself unto others let one not do, painful things oneself afflicting he who does not desire.
ai.translation: Let a man not do evil to others, if he does not wish painful consequences to afflict him.
ai.modern: துன்பம் தரும் செயல்கள் தன்னை வந்து தாக்குவதை விரும்பாதவன், தான் பிறருக்குத் தீமையான செயல்களைச் செய்யக்கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against committing evil deeds by appealing to self-interest. The word 'தீப்பால' refers to actions that are evil by nature, while 'நோய்ப்பால' refers to the painful consequences that naturally follow. The poet states that if a person does not wish to be afflicted by suffering, he must refrain from doing evil to others. The underlying principle is that the harm one inflicts on others will inevitably return to cause pain to oneself.

ai.literal: Whatever enmity even those who have incurred will escape; the enmity of deeds, without ceasing, having gone behind, will destroy.
ai.translation: People may escape whatever other enmity they have incurred, but the enmity of evil deeds will relentlessly pursue and destroy them.
ai.modern: எவ்வளவு பெரிய பகையை அடைந்தவரும் அதிலிருந்து தப்பிப் பிழைக்கலாம். ஆனால், தீய செயல்களால் வரும் பகையானது அழியாமல் பின் தொடர்ந்தே வந்து அழித்துவிடும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts ordinary enmity with the consequences of evil deeds. The word எனைப்பகை suggests that worldly enemies, no matter how powerful, can be evaded or overcome. However, வினைப்பகை (the enmity created by one's own bad actions) is inescapable. The phrase வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும் vividly describes this consequence as an immortal pursuer that tracks the wrongdoer down and destroys them.

ai.literal: Evil deeds those who did perishing shadow oneself without leaving foot having stayed like that.
ai.translation: Destruction will follow those who commit evil deeds, just as a person's shadow stays unfailingly at their feet.
ai.modern: தீய செயல்களைச் செய்தவர்கள் அழிவது, ஒருவருடைய நிழல் அவரை விட்டு விலகாமல் அவர் அடியிலேயே தங்கியிருப்பதைப் போன்றது.
ai.explanation: This couplet illustrates the inescapable nature of the consequences of evil deeds. The poet uses the powerful simile of a shadow that never leaves a person's feet to explain how destruction will inevitably follow those who commit evil. Just as one cannot outrun or detach from their own shadow, a wrongdoer cannot escape the ruin brought about by their own actions.

ai.literal: Oneself oneself lover if-is, whatever-measure even-one let-not-approach evil-deed's side.
ai.translation: If a man truly loves himself, let him not approach even the smallest measure of evil deeds.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தன்னைத் தான் விரும்புபவனாக இருந்தால், அவன் எந்த அளவிலும் தீய செயல்களின் பக்கம் செல்லக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: The couplet establishes a direct link between self-love and moral behavior. The phrase 'தன்னைத் தான் காதலன் ஆயின்' means 'if one is a lover of oneself,' implying a genuine desire for one's own safety and happiness. Because evil deeds inevitably bring suffering back to the doer, true self-interest requires avoiding them completely. Therefore, the text commands 'துன்னற்க' (do not approach) even the slightest association with the side of evil.

ai.literal: One who is hard to ruin that let one know, side having run evil deed he does not do if.
ai.translation: Know that a man is safe from ruin if he does not go astray to commit evil deeds.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் தவறான வழியில் சென்று தீய செயல்களைச் செய்யமாட்டான் என்றால், அவனுக்கு அழிவு வராது என்பதை அறிந்துகொள்க.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains that avoiding evil deeds is the surest way to protect oneself from destruction. The phrase 'மருங்கு ஓடி' means running to the side or going astray from the righteous path. If a person refuses to deviate from virtue to commit evil, they become 'அருங்கேடன்', meaning someone whose ruin is highly unlikely. Thus, moral integrity is presented as the ultimate shield against downfall.
